article.contentMarkdown:
# What to Write in a Diwali Card When Every Card Says the Same Thing

Write four things in order: a greeting line, one middle line only you could have written, a forward-looking close, and your name. The greeting and close are fixed language — light over darkness, prosperity, Lakshmi's blessing — costing about twelve words between them. The middle line is the card. Budget 35–45 words, which is what fits on a folded card without crowding the printed art.

The words are the slow part, not the design. On SubhSandesh the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 6.9 hours (sampled on /love-gf, n=914, measured 2026-08-19) — people keep returning to the wording. And 51.8% of shared pages open on a phone (17,101 of 33,007 views, measured 2026-08-19), so what you write is read in one screen, once. Below: the anatomy, the length budget, the wording for 6–10 November 2026, four recipient tiers and eight worked cards.

## The four parts of a Diwali card, and the one everybody skips

A Diwali card has a greeting, a personal middle, a forward-looking close and a sign-off. Three are pre-written for you; the middle is the only part carrying information, and the part people skip.

The greeting is the festival: "Shubh Deepavali", or "Happy Diwali to everyone at home". The close aims at the year rather than the night — "hope this one is easier than the last".

The middle is one or two sentences naming something true only of this recipient: something they did this year, a memory you both hold, or what you hope to do on Sunday 8 November. Skip it and you have posted a forward with a signature.

Card writers have always worked this way. Julia Gillen's study of [3,000 Edwardian postcards](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/65539/1/Writing_Edwardian_Postcards_post_print.pdf) (*Journal of Sociolinguistics*, 2013) found a traveller's card typically carried three things: where the sender had got to, a good wish, and a remark about the weather. News, then wish.

One upgrade: finish the middle with a question. In [three studies of live conversations](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/Huang%20et%20al%202017_6945bc5e-3b3e-4c0a-addd-254c9e603c60.pdf) (September 2017), people who asked more follow-up questions were better liked, and among speed daters an 8% difference in follow-up rate went with about one extra second date in an evening of 20 — correlational, the authors stress. A card is not a conversation, but a question earns a reply.

## How much to write: 35–45 words, and why the second paragraph weakens it

Five words of greeting, 20–30 of middle, eight of close, then your name. Few of Gillen's 3,000 postcards ran past 100 words, and those senders had more patience than you have on 8 November.

The second paragraph is where cards go wrong, because it is usually the first one explained. In a 2006 *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* paper, [Lyubomirsky, Sousa and Dickerhoof](https://sonjalyubomirsky.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/LSD2006.pdf) had 111 students write, talk or think about their happiest experience for 15 minutes a day over three days; those who wrote about and analysed a happy memory reported lower well-being four weeks later than those who simply replayed it.

That study measured the writer, not the reader, so I am borrowing the direction of the effect, not the finding. Still: name the memory, don't explain it. "The Diwali the power went out and we finished the puja on phone torches" beats a paragraph on what it meant.

Handwriting makes you commit. Smoker, Murphy and Rockwell's paper [comparing memory for handwriting versus typing](https://stars.library.ucf.edu/scopus2000/12667) (Human Factors and Ergonomics Society, 2009) reported better recall for handwritten than typed words, put down to the extra effort writing demands — which is why you choose fewer, better words on paper.

## Which of the five days it lands on: 6–10 November 2026

Diwali 2026 falls on **Sunday 8 November**, and the five-day span runs **6–10 November** — Dhanteras opens it on Friday, Bhai Dooj closes it on Tuesday. The close should match the day it is read.

A card read on 6 or 7 November is ahead of the festival: write forward, and put any invitation here — nobody accepts one on Sunday night.

A card opened on 8 November competes with the puja and a hundred forwarded images. Hold it to 30 words and put the middle line first, so the specific line is what the reader sees.

A card arriving on 9 or 10 November should not apologise. Drop "wishing you", which has expired, and ask instead: "How was Sunday — what did you cook?" Because Diwali 2026 is a Sunday, work cards must land by Thursday 5 or Friday 6 November; no office day falls inside the festival.

## Four tiers of recipient, four different cards

Indian Diwali card-giving runs across four tiers and one wording cannot serve all of them: family, neighbours, colleagues and clients, and the people who work in your home or building.

| Recipient tier | Words that fit | What the middle line names | If you send a link instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parents, siblings, grandparents | 45–60 | a shared memory, or a plan for Sunday 8 November | Works — 51.8% of shared pages are opened on a phone |
| Neighbours | 25–35 | the specific thing they did for you this year | Weak — you share a wall; hand it over |
| Colleagues, manager, clients | 20–30 | one piece of their work you actually saw | Works, but skip the password 44.3% of creators add |
| Landlord, house help, watchman | 15–25 | thanks for one concrete thing, and asks for nothing | No — a printed card handed over is the right object |

The fourth tier is written worst. A card to the person who cleans your flat should thank them for something specific and not perform generosity: fifteen words with their name spelled correctly does more than a paragraph.

## Eight Diwali card messages, written out

### 1. Parents, when you are not coming home

"Ma, Papa — Shubh Deepavali. I'll be on the call at 7, and I've told Priya she's doing the diya row on the balcony wall like you do. Save me some anarsa. Hope this year is kinder."

### 2. A sibling and their family, for Bhai Dooj on 10 November

"Didi — happy Diwali to all four of you. I still owe you the ₹3,000 you lent me in March and never mentioned once. Bhai Dooj on Tuesday: tilak on video, or in person?"

### 3. The neighbour who sends sweets over every year

"Shubh Deepavali to the Iyer family. Your besan ladoo arrived before our diyas were out again, which is becoming a tradition. We're home all Sunday evening if you and the girls want to come across. — Flat 402"

### 4. A colleague you actually work with

"Happy Diwali, Nikhil. The migration week in July would have gone badly without you on the late calls, and nobody said so at the time. Enjoy the five days — see you on the 11th."

### 5. A manager or client, with no assumption about faith

"Wishing you a bright Diwali and a good week with your family. Thank you for how you handled the October deadline — those two days made the difference to my team. — Anjali"

### 6. Your landlord

"Happy Diwali to you and your family. Thank you for getting the water pump fixed the same week I called in August. Wishing you a good year ahead. — Tenant, Flat 3B"

### 7. The person who cleans your flat

"Shubh Deepavali, Kamla ji. Thank you for a year of work, and for the day in June you stayed late when we had guests. Happy Diwali to your family. — from all of us at 402"

### 8. A friend whose year has been hard

"Thinking of you this Diwali, Sameer. No wishes for prosperity from me — this year has taken enough. I'm around all five days, phone on. Coffee on the 9th if you're up for it."

## Hindi or English, and the one-line rule for mixing them

One Hindi line per card, in the greeting or close, never the middle. The middle carries the specific detail, which belongs in whichever language you actually speak to this person; formal Hindi wrapped around a detail you'd say in English reads as a translation. Three lines that work, with transliteration and gloss:

- **शुभ दीपावली** (*Shubh Deepavali*) — "auspicious Deepavali". The safest greeting, for anyone.
- **दीपावली की हार्दिक शुभकामनाएँ** (*Deepavali ki haardik shubhkaamnayein*) — "heartfelt Deepavali wishes". Formal; fits a landlord or client.
- **आपकी बहुत याद आती है** (*Aapki bahut yaad aati hai*) — "we miss you very much". For the close of a family card, not a work one.

If your Devanagari is rusty, use Roman script: "Shubh Deepavali" reads as intended to everyone on this list, while a shakily formed Devanagari line pulls attention to the handwriting instead of the wish.

## When "may this Diwali bring you prosperity" lands badly

If the recipient's year contained an illness, a death or a job loss, the standard close reads as a scoreboard — prosperity is what the year withheld. Cut the wish, keep the middle: "Thinking of you this week, and I'm around all five days" does the job. A card should never be the first place you mention a loss; if you haven't called, call.

Be honest about what writing carries. In [*Perspectives on Psychological Science*](https://cssh.northeastern.edu/pandemic-teaching-initiative/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2020/10/Pennebaker-Expressive-Writing-in-Psychological-Science.pdf) in 2018, James Pennebaker put the average effect of expressive writing on health across more than 100 studies at about d = 0.16 — small, from private 15-minute sessions, measured on the writer. Four lines are not treatment. Write shorter, not deeper.

## When a card is the wrong choice

If you will be in the same room on 8 November, say it out loud. If the recipient has no smartphone, print it — that 51.8% phone-open rate is the wrong statistic for a grandparent without one.

And SubhSandesh has no Diwali design today. The nearest festival page is the [Holi greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/holi); the rest of the [template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) is built for birthdays, apologies and romance; for a partner the [romantic "I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) is what people use — 914 of 2,739 pages, 33.4% of everything and 39.7% of all views (measured 2026-08-19). For the fourth tier a link is the wrong object. Buy the card.

## Sources

- Gillen, "Writing Edwardian postcards", *Journal of Sociolinguistics*, September 2013 — [post-print](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/65539/1/Writing_Edwardian_Postcards_post_print.pdf)
- Huang et al., "It Doesn't Hurt to Ask", *JPSP*, September 2017 — [PDF](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/Huang%20et%20al%202017_6945bc5e-3b3e-4c0a-addd-254c9e603c60.pdf)
- Lyubomirsky, Sousa & Dickerhoof, *JPSP*, April 2006 — [PDF](https://sonjalyubomirsky.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/LSD2006.pdf)
- Pennebaker, "Expressive Writing in Psychological Science", 2018 — [PDF](https://cssh.northeastern.edu/pandemic-teaching-initiative/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2020/10/Pennebaker-Expressive-Writing-in-Psychological-Science.pdf)
- Smoker, Murphy & Rockwell, "Comparing Memory for Handwriting Versus Typing", 2009 — [UCF STARS](https://stars.library.ucf.edu/scopus2000/12667) (abstract only)

failed.why: Four of five sources would survive being moved to another keyword's post: question-asking, writing about happy memories, expressive writing and handwriting recall are all general mechanisms, not Diwali-card findings. Only Gillen (postcard conventions) is tied to the artefact. This is the same weakness recorded against the subject-test item above and is the post's main sourcing limitation, not a separate incident.

failed.item: metaTitle 50–60 characters, exact keyword in the first five words (hard cap 70)
failed.why: metaTitle is 56 characters with the exact keyword in the first six words, not five — "What to Write in a Diwali Card" is itself seven words because the keyword contains four function words. No shorter arrangement keeps the exact phrase intact.

failed.item: Slug short, hyphenated, lowercase, no stop words
failed.why: Slug carries four stop words (what, to, in, a) because it mirrors the exact keyword. It was pinned and Strapi-verified before drafting; changing it now desynchronises the filename, batch.json and the research brief. This item has now failed on most posts in this project whose keyword is a natural-language question, and needs a policy decision rather than a per-post fix.

failed.item: At least 2 sources pass the subject test — about siblings / ritual / distance / the language / the platform behaviour, not merely about India or the internet
failed.why: Only one source (Gillen on Edwardian postcards) is genuinely about the artefact this post is about — written greeting cards. The other four are about adjacent mechanisms: question-asking in conversation, writing about happy memories, expressive writing, and handwriting recall. Each is used for direction rather than as a finding about Diwali cards, and the body says so explicitly in three places. No study of Diwali card wording appears to exist; the searches tried are listed in the brief.

auditReport.honestAssessment: Every page on this query is a wishes inventory; none gives a word budget, an anatomy, a per-day rule for the five days, or a tier for household staff and building watchmen, which is a real part of Indian Diwali card-giving that the whole SERP ignores. The sourcing is the honest weakness: only one source is about greeting cards at all, and the other four are borrowed for the direction of an effect rather than a finding — which the body states in three places rather than hiding. No first-party fact is Diwali-specific, and the post has to admit there is no Diwali design, so for its fourth tier the correct advice is to buy a paper card rather than use our product.
